entries.4a842f980254836fd650b11db58c4a7293a76ee4: <div sID="gen11930" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="80" osisID="Ps.80" sID="Ps.80"/> <div eID="gen11930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11931" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11932" type="x-p"/> This psalm is much to the same purport with the foregoing. Some think it was penned upon occasion of the desolation and captivity of the ten tribes, as the foregoing psalm of the two. But many were the distresses of the Israel of God, many perhaps which are not recorded in the sacred history some whereof might give occasion for the drawing up of this psalm, which is proper to be sung in the day of Jacob's trouble, and if, in singing it, we express a true love to the church and a hearty concern for its interest, with a firm confidence in God's power to help it out of its greatest distresses, we make melody with our hearts to the Lord. The psalmist here, I. Begs for the tokens of God's presence with them and favour to them, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.1-Ps.80.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. He complains of the present rebukes they were under, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.4-Ps.80.7">ver. 4-7</reference>. III. He illustrates the present desolations of the church, by the comparison of a vine and a vineyard, which had flourished, but was now destroyed, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.8-Ps.80.16">ver. 8-16</reference>. IV. He concludes with prayer to God for the preparing of mercy for them and the preparing of them for mercy, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.17-Ps.80.19">ver. 17-19</reference>. This, as many psalms before and after, relates to the public interests of God's Israel, which ought to lie nearer to our hearts than any secular interest of our own.
entries.195068f11b86a809d4cde8cf553304bed23a0218: <div eID="gen11932" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11931" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Mournful Complaints.</title> <div sID="gen11933" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, thou that leadest Joseph like a flock; thou that dwellest <hi type="italic">between</hi> the cherubims, shine forth. <hi type="super">2</hi> Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh stir up thy strength, and come <hi type="italic">and</hi> save us. <hi type="super">3</hi> Turn us again, O God, and cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved. <hi type="super">4</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God of hosts, how long wilt thou be angry against the prayer of thy people? <hi type="super">5</hi> Thou feedest them with the bread of tears; and givest them tears to drink in great measure. <hi type="super">6</hi> Thou makest us a strife unto our neighbours: and our enemies laugh among themselves. <hi type="super">7</hi> Turn us again, O God of hosts, and cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved. <div eID="gen11933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11934" type="x-p"/> The psalmist here, in the name of the church, applies to God by prayer, with reference to the present afflicted state of Israel. <div eID="gen11934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11935" type="x-p"/> I. He entreats God's favour for them (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.1-Ps.80.2">v. 1, 2</reference>); that is all in all to the sanctuary when it is desolate, and is to be sought in the first place. Observe, 1. How he eyes God in his address as the Shepherd of Israel, whom he had called the <hi type="italic">sheep of his pasture</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.13">Ps. lxxix. 13</reference>), under whose guidance and care Israel was, as the sheep are under the care and conduct of the shepherd. Christ is the great and good Shepherd, to whom we may in faith commit the custody of his sheep that were given to him. He <hi type="italic">leads Joseph like a flock,</hi> to the best pastures, and out of the way of danger; if Joseph follow him not as obsequiously as the sheep do the shepherd, it is his own fault. He <hi type="italic">dwells between the cherubim,</hi> where he is ready to receive petitions and to give directions. The mercy-seat was between the cherubim; and it is very comfortable in prayer to look up to God as sitting on a throne of grace, and that it is so to us is owning to the great propitiation, for the mercy-seat was the propitiatory. 2. What he expects and desires from God, that he would give ear to the cry of their miseries and of their prayers, that he would shine forth both in his own glory and in favour and kindness to his people, that he would show himself and smile on them, that he would <hi type="italic">sir up his strength,</hi> that he would excite it and exert it. It had seemed to slumber: "Lord, awaken it." His cause met with great opposition and the enemies threatened to overpower it: "Lord, put forth thy strength so much the more, and come for salvation to us; be to thy people a powerful help and a present help; Lord, do this <hi type="italic">before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh,</hi>" that is, "In the sight of all the tribes of Israel; let them see it to their satisfaction." Perhaps these three tribes are named because they were the tribes which formed that squadron of the camp of Israel that in their march through the wilderness followed next after the tabernacle; so that before them the ark of God's strength rose to scatter their enemies. <div eID="gen11935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11936" type="x-p"/> II. He complains of God's displeasure against them. God was angry, and he dreads that more than any thing, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.4">v. 4</reference>. 1. It was great anger. He apprehended that God was <hi type="italic">angry against the prayer of his people,</hi> not only that he was angry notwithstanding their prayers, by which they hoped to turn away his wrath from them, but that he was angry with their prayers, though they were his own people that prayed. That God should be angry at the sins of his people and at the prayers of his enemies is not strange; but that he should be angry at the prayers of his people is strange indeed. He not only delayed to answer them (that he often does in love), but he was displeased at them. If he be really angry at the prayers of his people, we may be sure it is because they ask amiss, <reference osisRef="Jas.4.3">Jam. iv. 3</reference>. They pray, but they do not wrestle in prayer; their ends are not right, or there is some secret sin harboured and indulged in them; they do not lift up pure hands, or they lift them up with wrath and doubting. But perhaps it is only in their own apprehension; he seems angry with their prayers when really he is not; for thus he will try their patience and perseverance in prayer, as Christ tried the woman of Canaan when he said, <hi type="italic">It is not meet to take the children's bread and cast it to dogs.</hi> 2. It was anger that had continued a great while: "<hi type="italic">How long wilt thou be angry?</hi> We have still continued praying and yet are still under thy frowns." Now the tokens of God's displeasure which they had been long under were both their sorrow and shame. (1.) Their sorrow (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou feedest them with the bread of tears;</hi> they eat their meat from day to day in tears; this is the vinegar in which they <hi type="italic">dipped their morsel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.42.3">Ps. xlii. 3</reference>. They had tears given them to drink, not now and then a taste of that bitter cup, but in great measure. Note, There are many that spend their time in sorrow who yet shall spend their eternity in joy. (2.) It was their shame, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.6">v. 6</reference>. God, by frowning upon them, made them a strife unto their neighbours; each strove which should expose them most, and such a cheap and easy prey were they made to them that all the strife was who should have the stripping and plundering of them. Their enemies laughed among themselves to see the frights they were in, the straits they were reduced to, and the disappointments they met with. When God is displeased with his people we must expect to see them in tears and their enemies in triumph. <div eID="gen11936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11937" type="x-p"/> III. He prays earnestly for converting grace in order to their acceptance with God, and their salvation: <hi type="italic">Turn us again, O God!</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.80.3">v. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Turn us again, O God of hosts!</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.7">v. 7</reference>) and then <hi type="italic">cause thy face to shine and we shall be saved.</hi> It is the burden of the song, for we have it again, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.19">v. 19</reference>. They are conscious to themselves that they have gone astray from God and their duty, and have turned aside into sinful ways, and that it was this that provoked God to hide his face from them and to give them up into the hand of their enemies; and therefore they desire to begin their work at the right end: "Lord, turn us to thee in a way of repentance and reformation, and then, no doubt, thou wilt return to us in a way of mercy and deliverance." Observe, 1. No salvation but from God's favour: "<hi type="italic">Cause thy face to shine,</hi> let us have thy love and the light of thy countenance, and then we shall be saved." 2. No obtaining favour with God unless we be converted to him. We must turn again to God from the world and the flesh, and then he will cause his face to shine upon us. 3. No conversion to God but by his own grace; we must frame our doings to turn to him (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.4">Hos. v. 4</reference>) and then pray earnestly for his grace, <hi type="italic">Turn thou me, and I shall be turned,</hi> pleading that gracious promise (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.23">Prov. i. 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">Burn you at my reproof; behold, I will pour out my Spirit unto you.</hi> The prayer here is for a national conversion; in this method we must pray for national mercies, that what is amiss may be amended, and then our grievances would be soon redressed. National holiness would secure national happiness.
entries.fc45b626641e52afd1971a585887d8f3424f69e2: <div eID="gen11937" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Desolated Vine.</title> <div sID="gen11938" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: thou hast cast out the heathen, and planted it. <hi type="super">9</hi> Thou preparedst <hi type="italic">room</hi> before it, and didst cause it to take deep root, and it filled the land. <hi type="super">10</hi> The hills were covered with the shadow of it, and the boughs thereof <hi type="italic">were like</hi> the goodly cedars. 11 She sent out her boughs unto the sea, and her branches unto the river. <hi type="super">12</hi> Why hast thou <hi type="italic">then</hi> broken down her hedges, so that all they which pass by the way do pluck her? <hi type="super">13</hi> The boar out of the wood doth waste it, and the wild beast of the field doth devour it. <hi type="super">14</hi> Return, we beseech thee, O God of hosts: look down from heaven, and behold, and visit this vine; 15 And the vineyard which thy right hand hath planted, and the branch <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou madest strong for thyself. 16 <hi type="italic">It is</hi> burned with fire, <hi type="italic">it is</hi> cut down: they perish at the rebuke of thy countenance. <hi type="super">17</hi> Let thy hand be upon the man of thy right hand, upon the son of man <hi type="italic">whom</hi> thou madest strong for thyself. <hi type="super">18</hi> So will not we go back from thee: quicken us, and we will call upon thy name. <hi type="super">19</hi> Turn us again, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God of hosts, cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved. <div eID="gen11938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11939" type="x-p"/> The psalmist is here presenting his suit for the Israel of God, and pressing it home at the throne of grace, pleading with God for mercy and grace for them. The church is here represented as a vine (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.8">v. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.14">14</reference>) and a vineyard, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.15">v. 15</reference>. The root of this vine is Christ, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.18">Rom. xi. 18</reference>. The branches are believers, <reference osisRef="John.15.5">John xv. 5</reference>. The church is like a vine, weak and needing support, unsightly and having an unpromising outside, but spreading and fruitful, and its fruit most excellent. The church is a choice and noble vine; we have reason to acknowledge the goodness of God that he has planted such a vine in the wilderness of this world, and preserved it to this day. Now observe here, <div eID="gen11939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11940" type="x-p"/> I. How the vine of the Old-Testament church was planted at first. It was <hi type="italic">brought out of Egypt</hi> with a high hand; <hi type="italic">the heathen were cast out</hi> of Canaan to make room for it, seven nations to make room for that one. <hi type="italic">Thou didst sweep before it</hi> (so some read <reference osisRef="Ps.80.9">v. 9</reference>), to make clear work; the nations were swept away as dirt with the besom of destruction. God, having made room for it, and planted it, cause it to take deep root by a happy establishment of their government both in church and state, which was so firm that, though their neighbours about them often attempted it, they could not prevail to pluck it up. <div eID="gen11940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11941" type="x-p"/> II. How it spread and flourished. 1. The land of Canaan itself was fully peopled. At first they were not so numerous as to replenish it, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.29">Exod. xxiii. 29</reference>. But in Solomon's time <hi type="italic">Judah and Israel were many as the sand of the sea;</hi> the land was filled with them, and yet such a fruitful land that it was not over-stocked, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.10">v. 10</reference>. The hills of Canaan were covered with their shadow, and the branches, though they extended themselves far, like those of the vine, yet were not weak like them, but as strong as those of the goodly cedars. Israel not only had abundance of men, but those mighty men of valour. 2. They extended their conquests and dominion to the neighbouring countries (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">She sent out her boughs to the sea,</hi> the great sea westward, and <hi type="italic">her branches to the river,</hi> to the river of Egypt southward, the river of Damascus northward, or rather the river Euphrates eastward, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">Gen. xv. 18</reference>. Nebuchadnezzar's greatness is represented by a flourishing tree, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.20-Dan.4.21">Dan. iv. 20, 21</reference>. But it is observable here concerning this vine that it is praised for its <hi type="italic">shadow,</hi> its <hi type="italic">boughs,</hi> and its <hi type="italic">branches,</hi> but not a word of its fruit, for <hi type="italic">Israel was an empty vine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.10.1">Hos. x. 1</reference>. God came looking for grapes, but, behold, wild grapes, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.2">Isa. v. 2</reference>. And, if a vine do not bring forth fruit, no tree so useless, so worthless, <reference osisRef="Ezek.15.2">Ezek. xv. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.15.6">6</reference>. <div eID="gen11941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11942" type="x-p"/> III. How it was wasted and ruined: "Lord, thou hast done great things for this vine, and why shall it be all undone again? If it were a plant not of God's planting, it were not strange to see it rooted up; but will God desert and abandon that which he himself gave being to?" <reference osisRef="Ps.80.12">v. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Why hast thou then broken down her hedges?</hi> There was a good reason for this change in God's way towards them. This noble vine had become <hi type="italic">the degenerate plant of a strange vine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.21">Jer. ii. 21</reference>), to the reproach of its great owner, and then no marvel if he <hi type="italic">took away its hedge</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.5">Isa. v. 5</reference>); yet God's former favours to this vine are urged as pleas in prayer to God, and improved as encouragements to faith, that, notwithstanding all this, God would not wholly cast them off. Observe, 1. The malice and enmity of the Gentile nations against Israel. As soon as ever God <hi type="italic">broke down their hedges</hi> and left them exposed troops of enemies presently broke in upon them, that waited for an opportunity to destroy them. Those that passed by the way plucked at them; the <hi type="italic">board out of the wood</hi> and the <hi type="italic">wild beast of the field</hi> were ready to ravage it, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.13">v. 13</reference>. But, 2. See also the restraint which these cruel enemies were under; for till God had <hi type="italic">broken down their hedges</hi> they could not pluck a leaf of this vine. The devil could not hurt Job so long as God continued the <hi type="italic">hedge round about him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.1.10">Job i. 10</reference>. See how much it is the interest of any people to keep themselves in the favour of God and then they need not fear any wild beast of the field, <reference osisRef="Job.5.23">Job v. 23</reference>. If we provoke God to withdraw, <hi type="italic">our defence has departed from us,</hi> and we are undone. The deplorable state of Israel is described (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">It is burnt with fire; it is cut down;</hi> the people are treated like thorns and briers, that are nigh unto cursing and whose end is to be burned, and no longer like vines that are protected and cherished. They perish not through the rage of the wild beast and the boar, but <hi type="italic">at the rebuke of thy countenance;</hi> that was it which they dreaded and to which they attributed all their calamities. It is well or ill with us according as we are under God's smiles or frowns. <div eID="gen11942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11943" type="x-p"/> IV. What their requests were to God hereupon. 1. That God would help the vine (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.14-Ps.80.15">v. 14, 15</reference>), that he would graciously take cognizance of its case and do for it as he thought fit: "<hi type="italic">Return, we beseech thee, O Lord of hosts!</hi> for thou hast seemed to go away from us. <hi type="italic">Look down from heaven,</hi> to which thou hast retired,—from heaven, that place of prospect, whence thou seest all the wrongs that are done us, that place of power, whence thou canst send effectual relief,—from heaven, where thou hast prepared thy throne of judgment, to which we appeal, and where thou hast prepared a better country for those that are Israelites indeed,—thence give a gracious look, thence make a gracious visit, to this vine. Take our woeful condition into thy compassionate consideration, and for the particular fruits of thy pity we refer ourselves to thee. Only behold the vineyard, or rather the root, which <hi type="italic">thy right hand hath planted,</hi> and which therefore we hope thy right hand will protect, that <hi type="italic">branch which thou madest strong for thyself,</hi> to show forth thy praise (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.21">Isa. xliii. 21</reference>), that with the fruit of it thou mightest be honoured. Lord, it is formed by thyself and for thyself, and therefore it may with a humble confidence be committed to thyself and to thy own care." <hi type="italic">As for God, his work is perfect.</hi> What we read the <hi type="italic">branch</hi> in the Hebrew is the <hi type="italic">son (Ben</hi>), whom in thy counsel thou hast made strong for thyself. That branch was to come out of the stock of Israel (<hi type="italic">my servant the branch,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.3.8">Zech. iii. 8</reference>), and therefore, till he should come, Israel in general, and the house of David in particular, must be preserved, and upheld, and kept in being. <hi type="italic">He is the true vine,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.15.1">John xv. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Isa. xi. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Destroy it not for that blessing is in it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.65.8">Isa. lxv. 8</reference>. 2. That he would help the vine-dresser (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.17-Ps.80.18">v. 17, 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Let thy hand be upon the man of thy right hand,</hi>" that king (whoever it was) of the house of David that was now to go in and out before them; "let thy hand be upon him, not only to protect and cover him, but to own him, and strengthen him, and give him success." We have this phrase, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.28">Ezra vii. 28</reference>, <hi type="italic">And I was strengthened as the hand of the Lord my God was upon me.</hi> Their king is called the <hi type="italic">man of God's right hand</hi> as he was the representative of their state, which was dear to God, as his Benjamin, the <hi type="italic">son of his right hand,</hi> as he was president in their affairs and an instrument in God's right hand of much good to them, defending them from themselves and from their enemies and directing them in the right way, and as he was under-shepherd under him who was the great shepherd of Israel. Princes, who have power, must remember that they are <hi type="italic">sons of men,</hi> of <hi type="italic">Adam</hi> (so the word is), that, if they are strong, it is God that has made them strong, and he has made them so for himself, for they are his ministers to serve the interests of his kingdom among men, and, if they do this in sincerity, <hi type="italic">his hand shall be upon them;</hi> and we should pray in faith that it may be so, adding this promise, that, if God will adhere to our governors, we will adhere to him: <hi type="italic">So will not we go back from thee;</hi> we will never desert a cause which we see that God espouses and is the patron of. Let God be our leader and we will follow him. Adding also this prayer, "<hi type="italic">Quicken us,</hi> put life into us, revive our dying interests, revive our drooping spirits, and then <hi type="italic">we will call upon thy name.</hi> We will continue to do so upon all occasions, having found it not in vain to do so." We cannot call upon God's name in a right manner unless he quicken us; but it is he that puts life into our souls, that puts liveliness into our prayers. But many interpreters, both Jewish and Christian, apply this to the Messiah, the Son of David, the protector and Saviour of the church and the keeper of the vineyard. (1.) He is the man of God's right hand, to whom he has <hi type="italic">sworn by his right hand</hi> (so the Chaldee), whom he has exalted to his right hand, and who is indeed his right hand, the arm of the Lord, for all power is given to him. (2.) He is that son of man whom he <hi type="italic">made strong for himself,</hi> for the glorifying of his name and the advancing of the interests of his kingdom among men. (3.) God's hand is upon him throughout his whole undertaking, to bear him out and carry him on, to protect and animate him, that the <hi type="italic">good pleasure of the Lord might prosper in his hand.</hi> (4.) The stability and constancy of believers are entirely owing to the grace and strength which are laid up for us in Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.28">Ps. lxviii. 28</reference>. In him is our strength found, by which we are enabled to persevere to the end. Let thy hand be upon him; on him let our help be laid who is mighty; let him be made able to save to the uttermost and that will be our security; <hi type="italic">so will not we go back from thee.</hi> <div eID="gen11943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11944" type="x-p"/> Lastly, The psalm concludes with the same petition that had been put up twice before, and yet it is no vain repetition (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Turn us again.</hi> The title given to God rises, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.3">v. 3</reference>, <hi type="italic">O God!</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.80.7">v. 7</reference>, <hi type="italic">O God of hosts!</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.80.19">v. 19</reference>, <hi type="italic">O Lord (Jehovah) God of hosts!</hi> When we come to God for his grace, his good-will towards us and his good work in us, we should pray earnestly, continue instant in prayer, and pray more earnestly.  <chapter eID="Ps.80"/> <div eID="gen11944" type="x-p"/>

entries.320e314b7bb1d49358217bc561395c2facaeddc6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6430"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 80</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.80.1-Ps.80.19">Psa 80:1-19</reference>. Shoshannim--"Lilies" (see on <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">Psa 45:1</reference>, title). Eduth--Testimony, referring to the topic as a testimony of God to His people (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.19.7">Psa 19:7</reference>). This Psalm probably relates to the captivity of the ten tribes, as the former to that of Judah. Its complaint is aggravated by the contrast of former prosperity, and the prayer for relief occurs as a refrain through the Psalm.</title> <div sID="gen9848" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6430"/><hi type="bold">1-2. Joseph--</hi>for Ephraim (<reference osisRef="1Chr.7.20-1Chr.7.29">1Ch 7:20-29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.67">Psa 78:67</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.8">Re 7:8</reference>), for Israel.<div eID="gen9848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9849" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Shepherd--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.49.24">Ge 49:24</reference>).<div eID="gen9849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">leadest, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.77.20">Psa 77:20</reference>).<div eID="gen9850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9851" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwellest ... cherubim--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.25.20">Ex 25:20</reference>); the place of God's visible glory, whence He communed with the people (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.5">He 9:5</reference>).<div eID="gen9851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9852" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shine forth--</hi>appear (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.2">Psa 50:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.94.1">94:1</reference>). <div eID="gen9852" type="x-p"/>

entries.20427d9d19c3f90d911f797458d732cb052e797c: <div eID="gen21198" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21199" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21200" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21200" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21199" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21201" type="x-p"/> A prayer for the captives, <reference osisRef="Psa.80.1-Psa.80.3">Psa 80:1-3</reference>. A description of their miseries, <reference osisRef="Psa.80.4-Psa.80.7">Psa 80:4-7</reference>. Israel compared to a vineyard, <reference osisRef="Psa.80.8-Psa.80.14">Psa 80:8-14</reference>. Its desolate state, and a prayer for its restoration, <reference osisRef="Psa.80.15-Psa.80.19">Psa 80:15-19</reference>. <div eID="gen21201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21202" type="x-p"/> The title: see Psalm 45, <reference osisRef="Psa.60.1-Psa.60.12">Psa 60:1-12</reference>, and 69, where every thing material is explained. This Psalm seems to have been written on the same occasion with the former. One ancient MS. in the public library in Cambridge writes the eightieth and the seventy-ninth all as one Psalm; the subject-matter is precisely the same - was made on the same occasion, and probably by the same author. <div eID="gen21202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21203" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21204" type="x-p"/> O Shepherd of Israel - The subject continued from the last verse of the preceding Psalm. <div eID="gen21204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21205" type="x-p"/> Leadest Joseph - Israel and Joseph mean here the whole of the Jewish tribes; all were at this time in captivity; all had been the people of the Lord; all, no doubt, made supplication unto him now that his chastening hand was upon them; and for all the psalmist makes supplication. <div eID="gen21205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21206" type="x-p"/> That dwellest between the cherubims - It was between the cherubim, over the cover of the ark, called the propitiatory or mercy-seat, that the glory of the Lord, or symbol of the Divine Presence, appeared. It is on this account that the Lord is so often said to dwell between the cherubim. Of these symbolical beings there is a long and painful account, or system of conjectures, in Parkhurst's Hebrew Lexicon, of about twenty quarto pages, under the word כרב carab. <div eID="gen21206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21207" type="x-p"/> Shine forth - Restore thy worship; and give us such evidences of thy presence now, as our fathers had under the first tabernacle, and afterwards in the temple built by Solomon.
entries.2d3acde1a3244f5af2ec327511508289cf46cbee: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21208" type="x-p"/> Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh - It is supposed that these three tribes represent the whole, Benjamin being incorporated with Judah, Manasseh comprehending the country beyond Jordan, and Ephraim all the rest - Dodd.
entries.3773850ff9332079144c9ff761e862afb07b3dc7: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21209" type="x-p"/> Turn us again - השיבנו hashibenu, convert or restore us. There are four parts in this Psalm, three of which end with the above words; see the third, seventh, and nineteenth verses; and one with words similar, <reference osisRef="Psa.80.14">Psa 80:14</reference>.
entries.0436067ed8a96a12ae30fc3839dadac1b62232f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21210" type="x-p"/> Thou feedest them with the bread of tears - They have no peace, no comfort, nothing but continual sorrow. <div eID="gen21210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21211" type="x-p"/> In great measure - שליש shalish, threefold. Some think it was a certain measure used by the Chaldeans, the real capacity of which is not known. others think it signifies abundance or abundantly.
entries.46209fa867204702a2a7c824f43676e63e4682ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21212" type="x-p"/> Thou makest us a strife - The neighboring districts have a controversy about us; we are a subject of contention to them. A people so wonderfully preserved, and so wonderfully punished, is a mystery to them. They see in us both the goodness and severity of God. Or, all the neighboring nations join together to malign and execrate us. We are hated by all; derided and cursed by all.
entries.5f4d3641a13df862313b600159e31490e0ed72c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21213" type="x-p"/> Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt - This is a most elegant metaphor, and every where well supported. The same similitude is used by Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.1">Isa 5:1</reference>, etc.; by Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.21">Jer 2:21</reference>; by Ezekiel, <reference osisRef="Eze.17.5">Eze 17:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.17.6">Eze 17:6</reference>; by Hosea, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.1">Hos 10:1</reference>; by Joel, <reference osisRef="Joe.1.7">Joe 1:7</reference>; by Moses, <reference osisRef="Deu.32.32">Deu 32:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.32.33">Deu 32:33</reference>; and often by our Lord himself, <reference osisRef="Mat.20.1">Mat 20:1</reference>, etc.; <reference osisRef="Mat.21.33">Mat 21:33</reference>, etc.; <reference osisRef="Mar.12.1">Mar 12:1</reference>, etc. And this was the ordinary figure to represent the Jewish Church. We may remark several analogies here: - <div eID="gen21213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21214" type="x-p"/> 1. This vine was brought out of Egypt that it might be planted in a better and more favorable soil. The Israelites were brought out of their Egyptian bondage that they might be established in the land of Canaan, where they might grow and flourish, and worship the true God. <div eID="gen21214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21215" type="x-p"/> 2. When the husbandman has marked out a proper place for his vineyard, he hews down and roots up all other trees; gathers out the stones, brambles, etc., that might choke the young vines, and prevent them from being fruitful, So God cast out the heathen nations from the land of Canaan, that his pure worship might be established, and that there might not remain there any incitements to idolatry.
entries.9bd737df50a727a85237fb3552125b08c9465389: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21216" type="x-p"/> Thou preparedst - before it - <div eID="gen21216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21217" type="x-p"/> 3. When the ground is properly cleared, then it is well digged and manured, and the vines are placed in the ground at proper distances, etc. So when God had cast out the heathen, he caused the land to be divided by lot to the different tribes, and then to the several families of which these tribes were composed. <div eID="gen21217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21218" type="x-p"/> And didst cause it to take deep root - <div eID="gen21218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21219" type="x-p"/> 4. By sheltering, propping up, and loosening the ground about the tender plants, they are caused to take a deep and firm rooting in the ground. Thus did God, by especial manifestations of his kind providence, support and protect the Israelites in Canaan; and by various religious ordinances, and civil institutions, he established them in the land; and, by the ministry of priests and prophets, did every thing necessary to make them morally fruitful. <div eID="gen21219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21220" type="x-p"/> It filled the land - <div eID="gen21220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21221" type="x-p"/> 5. To multiply vines, the gardener cuts off a shoot from the old tree, leaving a joint or knob both at top and bottom; then plants it in proper soil; the lower knob furnishes the roots, and the upper the shoot, which should be carefully trained as it grows, in order to form another vine. By these means one tree will soon form a complete vineyard, and multiply itself to any given quantity. Thus God so carefully, tenderly, and abundantly blessed the Israelites, that they increased and multiplied; and, in process of time, filled the whole land of Canaan. Vines are propagated, not only by cuttings, but by layers, seed, grafting, and inoculation.
entries.2a9e6cbfc045b3d796cfa1aa25ce65602e20b95f: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen21221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21222" type="x-p"/> The hills were covered - <div eID="gen21222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21223" type="x-p"/> 6. The vine, carefully cultivated in a suitable soil, may be spread to any extent. In the land of Judea it formed shades under which the people not only sheltered and refreshed themselves in times of sultry heats; but it is said they even ate, drank, and dwelt under the shelter of their vines. See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.25">1Kgs 4:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.4.4">Mic 4:4</reference>; 1 Maccabees 14:12. God so blessed the Jews, particularly in the days of David and Solomon, that all the neighboring nations were subdued - the Syrians, Idumeans, Philistines, Moabites, and Ammonites.
entries.911ca7ebdc069bf78fa56f9d6c723b2f7849d7af: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen21223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21224" type="x-p"/> She sent out her boughs unto the sea and her branches unto the river - The Israelitish empire extended from the River Euphrates on the east to the Mediterranean Sea on the west, and from the same Euphrates on the north of the promised land to its farthest extent on the south; Syria bounding the north, and Arabia and Egypt the south. And this was according to the promises which God had made to the fathers, <reference osisRef="Exo.23.31">Exo 23:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.11.24">Deu 11:24</reference>.
entries.c47df02502bbdba76981750d86133349b967b16e: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen21224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21225" type="x-p"/> Why hast thou broken down - <div eID="gen21225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21226" type="x-p"/> 7. When a vineyard is planted, it is properly fenced to preserve it from being trodden down, or otherwise injured by beasts, and to protect the fruit from being taken by the unprincipled passenger. So God protected Jerusalem and his temple by his own almighty arm; and none of their enemies could molest them as long as they had that protection. As it was now spoiled, it was a proof that that protection had been withdrawn; therefore the psalmist addresses the Lord with, "Why hast thou broken down her hedges?" Had God continued his protection, Jerusalem would not have been destroyed.
entries.64cb073b4fb31be56802539a0c873c578ec2da22: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen21226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21227" type="x-p"/> The boar out of the wood - Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, who was a fierce and cruel sovereign. The allusion is plain. The wild hops and buffaloes make sad havoc in the fields of the Hindoos, and in their orchards: to keep them out, men are placed at night on covered stages in the fields.
entries.8f38cd099417ce1820588e622d2aef88d25f9131: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen21227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21228" type="x-p"/> Return - O God of hosts - Thou hast abandoned us, and therefore our enemies have us in captivity. Come back to us, and we shall again be restored. <div eID="gen21228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21229" type="x-p"/> Behold, and visit this vine - Consider the state of thy own people, thy own worship, thy own temple. Look down! Let thine eye affect thy heart.
entries.a30867f5daa2190de1064687ffaa95008f7ad1ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen21229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21230" type="x-p"/> The vineyard which thy right hand hath planted - Thy holy and pure worship which thy Almighty power had established in this city. <div eID="gen21230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21231" type="x-p"/> And the branch - thou madest strong for thy self - The original ועל בן veal ben, "and upon the Son whom thou hast strengthened for thyself." Many have thought that the Lord Jesus is meant. And so the Chaldee understood it, as it translates the passage thus: ועל מלכא משיחא veal Malca Meshicha, And upon the King Messiah, whom thou hast strengthened for thyself." The Syriac, Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic, have, "the Son of man,' as in the seventeenth verse. Eighteen of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. have בן אדם ben Adam, "Son of man," and as the Versions have all the same reading, it was probably that of the original copies. As Christ seems here to be intended, this is the first place in the Old Testament where the title Son of man is applied to him. The old Psalter understands this of setting Christ at the right hand of God.
entries.3995da315d1be5b3e6c4e8074537a47b1ffdd2a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen21231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21232" type="x-p"/> The man of thy right hand - The only person who can be said to be at the right hand of God as intercessor, is Jesus the Messiah. Let him become our Deliverer: appoint him for this purpose, and let his strength be manifested In our weakness! By whom are the Jews to be restored, if indeed they ever be restored to their own land, but by Jesus Christ? By Him alone can they find mercy; through Him alone can they ever be reconciled to God.
entries.ae2803d00f9961a5dae316b51ac60f579cf230e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen21232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21233" type="x-p"/> So wilt not we go back from thee - We shall no more become idolaters: and it is allowed on all hands that the Jews were never guilty of idolatry after their return from the Babylonish captivity. <div eID="gen21233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21234" type="x-p"/> Quicken us - Make us alive, for we are nearly as good as dead. <div eID="gen21234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21235" type="x-p"/> We will call upon they name - We will invoke thee. Thou shalt be for ever the object of our adoration, and the center of all our hopes.
entries.479f4ab7d2623509731945fb4e8a69b6d4ead588: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen21235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21236" type="x-p"/> Turn as again - Redeem us from this captivity. <div eID="gen21236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21237" type="x-p"/> O Lord God of hosts - Thou who hast all power in heaven and earth, the innumerable hosts of both worlds being at thy command. <div eID="gen21237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21238" type="x-p"/> Cause thy face to shine - Let us know that thou art reconciled to us. Let us once more enjoy thy approbation. Smile upon thy poor rebels, weary of their sins, and prostrate at thy feet, imploring mercy. <div eID="gen21238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21239" type="x-p"/> And we shall be saved - From the power and oppression of the Chaldeans, from the guilt and condemnation of our sins, and from thy wrath and everlasting displeasure. Thus, O God, save Us!  <chapter eID="Ps.80"/> <div eID="gen21239" type="x-p"/>

entries.4124c1ca8c6657d6b9ac86c7e6e957d679e2837d: <div eID="gen9813" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Prayer for Jahve’s Vine</title> <div sID="gen9814" type="x-p"/> With the words <hi type="italic">We are Thy people and the flock of Thy pasture</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.1-Ps.79.13">Psa 79:1-13</reference> closes; and Psalms 80 begins with a cry to the Shepherd of Israel. Concerning the inscription of the Psalm: <hi type="italic">To be practised after the “Lilies, the testimony...,” by Asaph, a Psalm</hi>, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">Psa 45:1</reference>, <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, p. 45f. The lxx renders, εἰς τὸ τέλος (unto the end), ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀλλοιωθησομένων (which is unintelligible and ungrammatical = אל־שׁשּׂנים), μαρτύριον τῷ Ἀσάφ (as the accentuation also unites these words closely by <hi type="italic">Tarcha</hi>), ψαλμός ὑπὲρ τοῦ Ἀσσυρίου (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.76.1">Psa 76:1</reference>), perhaps a translation of אל־אשׁור, an inscribed note which took the “boar out of the forest” as an emblem of Assyria. This hint is important. It solves the riddle why Joseph represents all Israel in <reference osisRef="Ps.80.2">Psa 80:2</reference>, and why the tribes of Joseph in particular are mentioned in <reference osisRef="Ps.80.3">Psa 80:3</reference>, and why in the midst of these Benjamin, whom like descent from Rachel and chagrin, never entirely overcome, on account of the loss of the kingship drew towards the brother-tribes of Joseph. Moreover the tribe of Benjamin had only partially remained to the house of David since the division of the kingdom,<note placement="foot">It is true we read that Benjamin stood on the side of Rehoboam with Judah after the division of the kingdom (1Ki 12:21), Judah and Benjamin appear as parts of the kingdom of Judah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.3">2Ch 11:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.23">2Ch 11:23</reference>; 2Ch 15:8., and frequently); but if, according to 1Ki 11:13, 1Ki 11:32, 1Ki 11:36, only שׁבט אחד remains to the house of David, this is Judah, inasmuch as Benjamin did not remain entirely under the Davidic sceptre, and Simeon is to be left out of account (cf. <hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>, S. 603); the Benjamitish cities of Bethel, Gilgal, and Jericho belonged to the northern kingdom, but, as in the case of Rama (1Ki 15:21.), not without being contested (cf. e.g., <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.19">2Ch 13:19</reference>); the boundaries were therefore fluctuating, vid., Ewald, <hi type="italic">Geschichte des Volkes Israel</hi> (3rd ed.), S. 439-441.</note> so that this triad is to be regarded as an expansion of the “Joseph” (v. 20. After the northern kingdom had exhausted its resources in endless feuds with Damascene Syria, it succumbed to the world-wide dominion of Assyria in the sixth year of Hezekiah, in consequence of the heavy visitations which are closely associated with the names of the Assyrian kings Pul, Tiglath-pileser, and Shalmaneser. The psalmist, as it seems, prays in a time in which the oppression of Assyria rested heavily upon the kingdom of Ephraim, and Judah saw itself threatened with ruin when this bulwark should have fallen. We must not, however, let it pass without notice that our Psalm has this designation of the nation according to the tribes of Joseph in common with other pre-exilic Psalms of Asaph (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.16">Psa 77:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.9">Psa 78:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.81.6">Psa 81:6</reference>). It is a characteristic belonging in common to this whole group of Psalms. Was Asaph, the founder of this circle of songs, a native, perhaps, of one of the Levite cities of the province of the tribe of Ephraim or Manasseh? <div eID="gen9814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9815" type="x-p"/> The Psalm consists of five eight-line strophes, of which the first, second, and fifth close with the refrain, “Elohim, restore us, let Thy countenance shine forth, then shall we be helped!” This prayer grows in earnestness. The refrain begins the first time with <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi>, the second time with <hi type="italic">Elohim Tsebaôth</hi>, and the third time with a threefold <hi type="italic">Jahve Elohim Tsebaôth</hi>, with which the second strophe (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.5">Psa 80:5</reference>) also opens. <div eID="gen9815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9816" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.80.2-Ps.80.3">Psa 80:2-3</reference> The first strophe contains nothing but petition. First of all the nation is called <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> as springing from Jacob; then, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.81.6">Psa 81:6</reference>, <hi type="italic">Joseph</hi>, which, where it is distinct from <hi type="italic">Jacob</hi> or <hi type="italic">Judah</hi>, is the name of the kingdom of the ten tribes (vid., Caspari on Oba 1:18), or at least of the northern tribes (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.16">Psa 77:16</reference>; Psa 78:67.). <reference osisRef="Ps.80.3">Psa 80:3</reference> shows that it is also these that are pre-eminently intended here. The fact that in the blessing of Joseph, Jacob calls God a Shepherd (רעה), <reference osisRef="Gen.48.15">Gen 48:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.49.24">Gen 49:24</reference>, perhaps has somewhat to do with the choice of the first two names. In the third, the sitting enthroned in the sanctuary here below and in the heaven above blend together; for the Old Testament is conscious of a mutual relationship between the earthly and the heavenly temple (היכל) until the one merges entirely in the other. The cherûbim, which God enthrones, i.e., upon which He sits enthroned, are the bearers of the chariot (מרכבה) of the Ruler of the world (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.18.11">Psa 18:11</reference>). With הופיעה (from יפע, Arab. <hi type="italic">yf‛ , eminere , emicare</hi>, as in the Asaph <reference osisRef="Ps.50.2">Psa 50:2</reference>) the poet prays that He would appear in His splendour of light, i.e., in His fiery bright, judging, and rescuing doxa, whether as directly visible, or even as only recognisable by its operation. Both the comparison, “after the manner of a flock” and the verb נהג are Asaphic, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.52">Psa 78:52</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.26.1">Psa 26:1</reference>-12. Just so also the names given to the nation. The designation of Israel after the tribes of <hi type="italic">Ephraim</hi> and <hi type="italic">Manasseh</hi> attaches itself to the name <hi type="italic">Joseph</hi>; and the two take the brother after the flesh into their midst, of whom the beloved Rachel was the mother as well as of Joseph, the father of Ephraim and Manasseh. In Num. 2 also, these three are not separated, but have their camp on the west side of the Tabernacle. May God again put into activity - which is the meaning of עורר (<hi type="italic">excitare</hi>) in distinction from חעיר (<hi type="italic">expergefacere</hi>) - His גבורה, the need for the energetic intervention of which now makes itself felt, before these three tribes, i.e., by becoming their victorious leader. לכה is a summoning imperative.<note placement="foot">Not a pronoun: to Thee it belongs to be for salvation for us, as the Talmud, Midrash, and Masora (vid., Norzi) take it; wherefore in <hi type="italic">J. Succa</hi> 54 <hi type="italic">c</hi> it is straightway written לך. Such a לכה = לך is called in the language of the Masora, and even in the Midrash (<hi type="italic">Exod. Rabba</hi>, fol. 121), לכה ודאית (vid., Buxtorf, <hi type="italic">Tiberias</hi>, p. 245).</note> <div eID="gen9816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9817" type="x-p"/> Concerning ישׁעתה vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.3.3">Psa 3:3</reference>; the construction with <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> says as little against the accusative adverbial rendering of the <hi type="italic">ah</hi> set forth there as does the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of בּחרשׁה (in the wood) in <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.15">1Sa 23:15</reference>, vid., Böttcher’s <hi type="italic">Neue Aehrenlese</hi>, Nos. 221, 384, 449. It is not a bringing back out of the Exile that is prayed for by השׁתבנוּ, for, according to the whole impression conveyed by the Psalm, the people are still on the soil of their fatherland; but in their present feebleness they are no longer like themselves, they stand in need of divine intervention in order again to attain a condition that is in harmony with the promises, in order to become themselves again. May God then cause His long hidden countenance to brighten and shine upon them, then shall they be helped as they desire (ונוּשׁעה).
entries.c4f1f8baede0cae602d0cde19dae00798d371430: <reference osisRef="Ps.80.4-Ps.80.7">Psa 80:4-7</reference> <div eID="gen9817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9818" type="x-p"/> In the second strophe there issues forth bitter complaint concerning the form of wrath which the present assumes, and, thus confirmed, the petition rises anew. The transferring of the smoking (עשׁן) of God’s nostrils = the hard breathing of anger (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.1">Psa 74:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.19">Deu 29:19</reference>), to God Himself is bold, but in keeping with the spirit of the Biblical view of the wrath of God (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.18.9">Psa 18:9</reference>), so that there is no need to avoid the expression by calling in the aid of the Syriac word עשׁן, to be strong, powerful (why art Thou hard, why dost Thou harden Thyself...). The perfect after עד־מתי has the sense of a present with a retrospective glance, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.10.3">Exo 10:3</reference>, cf. עד־אנה, to be understood after the analogy of חרה בּ (to kindle = to be angry against any one), for the prayer of the people is not an object of wrath, but only not a means of turning it aside. While the prayer is being presented, God veils Himself in the smoke of wrath, through which it is not able to penetrate. The lxx translators have read בתפלת עבדיך, for they render ἐπὶ τὴν προσευχήν τῶν δούλων σου (for which the common reading is τοῦ δούλου σου). Bread of tears is, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.42.4">Psa 42:4</reference>, bread consisting of tears; tears, running down in streams upon the lips of the praying and fasting one, are his meat and his drink. השׁקה with an accusative signifies to give something to drink, and followed by <hi type="italic">Beth</hi>, to give to drink by means of something, but it is not to be translated: <hi type="italic">potitandum das eis cum lacrymis trientem</hi> (De Dieu, von Ortenberg, and Hitzig). שׁלישׁ (Talmudic, a third part) is the accusative of more precise definition (Vatablus, Gesenius, Olshausen, and Hupfeld): by thirds (lxx ἐν μέτρῳ, Symmachus μέτρῳ); for a third of an ephah is certainly a very small measure for the dust of the earth (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.12">Isa 40:12</reference>), but a large one for tears. The neighbours are the neighbouring nations, to whom Israel is become מדון, an object, a butt of contention. In למו is expressed the pleasure which the mocking gives them.
entries.a9cc6b1540a36edec64a637d543c3164bca1c5a9: <reference osisRef="Ps.80.8-Ps.80.19">Psa 80:8-19</reference> <div eID="gen9818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9819" type="x-p"/> The complaint now assumes a detailing character in this strophe, inasmuch as it contrasts the former days with the present; and the ever more and more importunate prayer moulds itself in accordance therewith. The retrospective description begins, as is rarely the case, with the second <hi type="italic">modus</hi>, inasmuch as “the speaker thinks more of the bare nature of the act than of the time” (Ew. §136, <hi type="italic">b</hi>). As in the blessing of Jacob (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.22">Gen 49:22</reference>) Joseph is compared to the layer (בּן) of a fruitful growth (פּרת), whose shoots (בּנות) climb over the wall: so here Israel is compared to a vine (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.22">Gen 49:22</reference>; גּפן פּריּח, <reference osisRef="Ps.128.3">Psa 128:3</reference>), which has become great in Egypt and been transplanted thence into the Land of Promise. הסּיע, lxx μεταίρειν, as in <reference osisRef="Job.19.10">Job 19:10</reference>, perhaps with an allusion to the מסעים of the people journeying to Canaan (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.52">Psa 78:52</reference>).<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Exod. Rabba</hi>, ch. 44, with reference to this passage, says: “When husbandmen seek to improve a vine, what do they do? They root (עוקרין) it out of its place and plant (שׁותלין) it in another.” And <hi type="italic">Levit. Rabba</hi>, ch. 36, says: “As one does not plant a vine in a place where there are great, rough stones, but examines the ground and then plants it, so didst Thou drive out peoples and didst plant it,” etc.</note> <div eID="gen9819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9820" type="x-p"/> Here God made His vine a way and a place (פּנּהּ, to clear, from פּנה, to turn, turn aside, Arabic <hi type="italic">fanija</hi>, to disappear, pass away; root פן, to urge forward), and after He had secured to it a free soil and unchecked possibility of extension, it (the vine) rooted its roots, i.e., struck them ever deeper and wider, and filled the earth round about (cf. the antitype in the final days, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.6">Isa 27:6</reference>). The Israelitish kingdom of God extended itself on every side in accordance with the promise. תּשׁלּח (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.6">Eze 17:6</reference>, and vegetable שׁלח, a shoot) also has the vine as its subject, like תּשׁרשׁ. <reference osisRef="Ps.80.11-Ps.80.12">Psa 80:11-12</reference> state this in a continued allegory, by the “mountains” pointing to the southern boundary, by the “cedars” to the northern, by the “sea” to the western, and by the “river” (Euphrates) to the eastern boundary of the country (vid., <reference osisRef="Deut.11.24">Deu 11:24</reference> and other passages). צלּהּ and ענפיה are accusatives of the so-called more remote object (Ges. §143, 1). קציר is a cutting = a branch; יונקת, a (vegetable) sucker = a young, tender shoot; ארזי־אל, the cedars of Lebanon as being living monuments of the creative might of God. The allegory exceeds the measure of the reality of nature, inasmuch as this is obliged to be extended according to the reality of that which is typified and historical. But how unlike to the former times is the present! The poet asks “wherefore?” for the present state of things is a riddle to him. The surroundings of the vine are torn down; all who come in contact with it pluck it (ארה, to pick off, pluck off, Talmudic of the gathering of figs); the boar out of the wood (מיער with עין תלויה, <hi type="italic">Ajin</hi>)<note placement="foot">According to <hi type="italic">Kiddushin</hi>, 30 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, because this <hi type="italic">Ajin</hi> is the middle letter of the Psalter as the <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> of גחון, <reference osisRef="Lev.11.42">Lev 11:42</reference>, is the middle letter of the Tôra. One would hardly like to be at the pains of proving the correctness of this statement; nevertheless in the seventeenth century there lived one Laymarius, a clergyman, who was not afraid of this trouble, and found the calculations of the Masora (e.g., that אדני ה occurs 222 times) in part inaccurate; vid., <hi type="italic">Monatliche Unterredungen</hi>, 1691, S. 467, and besides, Geiger, <hi type="italic">Urschrift und Uebersetzungen der Bibel</hi>, S. 258f.)</note> cuts it off (כּרסם, formed out of כּסם = גּזם<note placement="foot">Saadia appropriately renders it Arab. <hi type="italic">yqrḍhâ</hi>, by referring, as does Dunash also, to the Talmudic קרסם, which occurs of ants, like Arab. <hi type="italic">qrḍ</hi>, of rodents. So <hi type="italic">Peah</hi> ii. §7, <hi type="italic">Menachoth</hi> 71 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, on which Rashi observes, “the locust (חגב) is accustomed to eat from above, the ant tears off the corn-stalk from below.” Elsewhere קירסם denotes the breaking off of dry branches from the tree, as זרד the removal of green branches.)</note> viz., with its tusks; and that which moves about the fields (vid., concerning זיז, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.11">Psa 50:11</reference>), i.e., the untractable, lively wild beast, devours it. Without doubt the poet associates a distinct nation with the wild boar in his mind; for animals are also in other instances the emblems of nations, as e.g., the leviathan, the water-serpent, the behemoth (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.6">Isa 30:6</reference>), and flies (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.18">Isa 7:18</reference>) are emblems of Egypt. The Midrash interprets it of Seîr-Edom, and זיז שׂדי, according to <reference osisRef="Gen.16.12">Gen 16:12</reference>, of the nomadic Arabs. <div eID="gen9820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9821" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ps.80.15">Psa 80:15</reference> the prayer begins for the third time with threefold urgency, supplicating for the vine renewed divine providence, and a renewal of the care of divine grace. We have divided the verse differently from the accentuation, since שׁוּב־נא הבּט is to be understood according to Ges. §142. The junction by means of ו is at once opposed to the supposition that וכּנּה in <reference osisRef="Ps.80.16">Psa 80:16</reference> signifies a slip or plant, <hi type="italic">plantam</hi> (Targum, Syriac, Aben-Ezra, Kimchi, and others), and that consequently the whole of <reference osisRef="Ps.80.16">Psa 80:16</reference> is governed by וּפקד. Nor can it mean its (the vine’s) stand or base, כּן (Böttcher), since one does not plant a “stand.” The lxx renders וכנה: καὶ κατάρτισαι, which is <hi type="italic">imper. aor</hi>. 1. <hi type="italic">med.,</hi> therefore in the sense of כּוננה.<note placement="foot">Perhaps the <hi type="italic">Caph majusculum</hi> is the result of an erasure that required to be made, vid., Geiger, <hi type="italic">Urschrift</hi>, S. 295. Accordingly the <hi type="italic">Ajin suspensum</hi> might also be the result of a later inserted correction, for there is a Phoenician inscription that has יר (wood, forest); vid., Levy, <hi type="italic">Phönizisches Wörterbuch</hi>, S. 22.</note> <div eID="gen9821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9822" type="x-p"/> But the alternation of על (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.2.11">Pro 2:11</reference>, and Arab. <hi type="italic">jn ‛lâ</hi>, to cover over) with the accusative of the object makes it more natural to derive כנה, not from כּנן = כּוּן, but from כּנן Arab. <hi type="italic">kanna</hi> = גּנן, to cover, conceal, protect (whence Arab. <hi type="italic">kinn</hi>, a covering, shelter, hiding-place): and protect him whom...or: protect what Thy right hand has planted. The pointing certainly seems to take כנה as the feminine of כּן (lxx, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.7">Dan 11:7</reference>, φυτόν); for an <hi type="italic">imperat. paragog.</hi> <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> of the form כּנּה does not occur elsewhere, although it might have been regarded by the punctuists as possible from the form גּל, <hi type="italic">volve</hi>, Psa 119:22. If it is regarded as impossible, then one might read כנּה. At any rate the word is imperative, as the following אשׁר, <hi type="italic">eum quem</hi>, also shows, instead of which, if כנה were a substantive, one would expect to find a relative clause without אשׁר, as in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.80.16">Psa 80:16</reference></hi>. Moreover <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.80.16">Psa 80:16</reference></hi> requires this, since פּקד על can only be used of visiting with punishment. And who then would the slip (branch) and the son of man be in distinction from the vine? If we take בנה as imperative, then, as one might expect, the vine and the son of man are both the people of God. The Targum renders <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.80.16">Psa 80:16</reference></hi> thus: “and upon the King Messiah, whom Thou hast established for Thyself,” after <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12">Psa 2:1-12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Dan 7:13</reference>; but, as in the latter passage, it is not the Christ Himself, but the nation out of which He is to proceed, that is meant. אמּץ has the sense of firm appropriation, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.44.14">Isa 44:14</reference>, inasmuch as the notion of making fast passes over into that of laying firm hold of, of seizure. Rosenmüller well renders it: <hi type="italic">quem adoptatum tot nexibus tibi adstrinxisti.</hi> <div eID="gen9822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9823" type="x-p"/> The figure of the vine, which rules all the language here, is also still continued in <reference osisRef="Ps.80.17">Psa 80:17</reference>; for the <hi type="italic">partt. fem.</hi> refer to גּפן ot refer, - the verb, however, may take the plural form, because those of Israel are this “vine,” which <hi type="italic">combusta igne, succisa</hi> (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.33.12">Isa 33:12</reference>; Aramaic, be cut off, tear off, in <reference osisRef="Ps.80.13">Psa 80:13</reference> the Targum word for ארה; Arabic, <hi type="italic">ksḥ</hi>, to clear away, peel off), is just perishing, or hangs in danger of destruction (יאבדוּ) before the threatening of the wrathful countenance of God. The absence of anything to denote the subject, and the form of expression, which still keeps within the circle of the figure of the vine, forbid us to understand this <reference osisRef="Ps.80.17">Psa 80:17</reference> of the extirpation of the foes. According to the sense תּהי־ידך על<note placement="foot">The תהי has <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi>, like שׂאו־זמרה (<reference osisRef="Ps.81.3">Psa 81:3</reference>), בני־נכר (<reference osisRef="Ps.144.7">Psa 144:7</reference>), and the like. This <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> beside the <hi type="italic">Shebâ</hi> (instead of beside the following vowel) belongs to the peculiarities of the metrical books, which in general, on account of their more melodious mode of delivery, have many such a <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> beside <hi type="italic">Shebâ</hi>, which does not occur in the prose books. Thus, e.g., יהוה and אלהים always have <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> beside the <hi type="italic">Shebâ</hi> when they have <hi type="italic">Rebia magnum</hi> without a conjunctive, probably because <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi> and <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi> had such a fulness of tone that a first stroke fell even upon the <hi type="italic">Shebâ</hi>-letters.</note> coincides with the supplicatory כנה על. It is Israel that is called בּן in <reference osisRef="Ps.80.16">Psa 80:16</reference>, as being the son whom Jahve has called into being in Egypt, and then called out of Egypt to Himself and solemnly declared to be His son on Sinai (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.22">Exo 4:22</reference>; Hos 11:1), and who is now, with a play upon the name of Benjamin in <reference osisRef="Ps.80.3">Psa 80:3</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.80.16">Psa 80:16</reference>), called אישׁ ימינך, as being the people which Jahve has preferred before others, and has placed at His right hand<note placement="foot">Pinsker punctuates thus: Let Thy hand be upon the man, Thy right hand upon the son of man, whom, etc.; but the impression that ימינך and אמצתה לך coincide is so strong, that no one of the old interpreters (from the lxx and Targum onwards) has been able to free himself from it.</note> for the carrying out of His work of salvation; who is called, however, at the same time בּן־אדם, because belonging to a humanity that is feeble in itself, and thoroughly conditioned and dependent. It is not the more precise designation of the “son of man” that is carried forward by ולא־נסוג, “and who has not drawn back from Thee” (Hupfeld, Hitzig, and others), but it is, as the same relation which is repeated in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.80.19">Psa 80:19</reference></hi> shows, the apodosis of the preceding petition: then shall we never depart from Thee; נסוג being not a participle, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.44.19">Psa 44:19</reference>, but a <hi type="italic">plene</hi> written voluntative: <hi type="italic">recedamus</hi>, vowing new obedience as thanksgiving of the divine preservation. To the prayer in <reference osisRef="Ps.80.18">Psa 80:18</reference> corresponds, then, the prayer תּחיּנוּ, which is expressed as future (which can rarely be avoided, Ew. §229), with a vow of thanksgiving likewise following: then will we call with Thy name, i.e., make it the medium and matter of solemn proclamation. In v. 20 the refrain of this Psalm, which is laid out as a trilogy, is repeated for the third time. The name of God is here threefold.  <chapter eID="Ps.80"/> <div eID="gen9823" type="x-p"/>

entries.f5fc46380f1735e7d1224c0f0d8562b562dd5a8a:
PSALM 80
This is a sorrowful prayer, in which the faithful beseech God that he would be graciously pleased to succor his afflicted Church. To excite him the more readily to grant them relief in their distressing circumstances, they compare these circumstances with the condition of the Church in her beginnings, when the Divine favor was conspicuously manifested towards her.
To the chief musician upon Sosannim Eduth. A Psalm of Asaph.
This psalm is almost similar to the preceding; but, in my apprehension it was composed in behalf of the ten tribes, after that kingdom began to be wasted by various calamities. It is not without reason that mention is expressly made of Joseph, Ephraim, and Manasseh. Some expositors allege, that in this there is an allusion to the situation and order of the camps of the chosen tribes in the wilderness, as described by Moses in Numbers 2:18-21; for Manasseh and Ephraim marched together on one side.
This is the opinion of Hammond, who supposes that this psalm “is a complaint of the troubles of God’s Church and people, probably in time of captivity, or by way of prediction of it.” “Why Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh, and no other, are here named,” says he, “must be learned from the order of the Israelites’ march in the wilderness, Numbers 2. For there, next after the ark, the pledge of God’s special presence and assistance, did these three tribes follow: ‘Then the tabernacle of the congregation shall set forward,’ etc., verse 17; ‘On the west side (i.e., next behind it) shall be the standard of the camp of Ephraim,’ verse 18; ‘and his host,’ etc., verse 19. ‘And by him shall be the tribe of Manasseh,’ verse 20; ‘and his host,’ etc., verse 21. ‘Then the tribe of Benjamin, and his host,’ verses 22, 23. Now the returning from the captivity, the desire whereof is the business of this psalm, being a parallel to the delivery from Egypt, God’s ‘leading them back, stirring up himself, and coming to save them,’ is very fitly. begged, and described in a style resembling the former rescue.” Merrick accounts for Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh, being particularly specified, by supposing the psalm to have been written at a time when some enemy was advancing towards these tribes, which were contiguously situated, or was directing his march to Jerusalem, through their territories. “Such an occasion,” he observes, “might make it very proper for the Psalmist to pray that the people of those tribes might particularly be made spectators of the divine interposition. If the psalm was not written on any such occasion, it may be most reasonable to suppose, that Benjamin, Joseph’s only brother by the same mother, and Ephraim and Manasseh his sons, are in the second verse equivalent to Joseph; who, in the preceding verse, represents the whole posterity of Israel.”
But it would have been strange to have passed over in silence the tribe of Judah, and also the holy city, and to have brought forward the tribes of Joseph, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Benjamin, had it not been intended to speak especially of the kingdom of Israel.
The argument which Calvin here adduces in support of the opinion, that this psalm relates to the ten tribes which constituted the kingdom of Israel, in contradistinction to the kingdom of Judah, is evidently inconclusive. He seems to have forgotten the fact that the tribe of Benjamin, which is expressly specified, did not belong to the kingdom of Israel, but formed a part of the kingdom of Judah, — a fact which is altogether destructive of the argument by which he attempts to prove that the psalm relates exclusively or especially to the kingdom of Israel. The whole of God’s ancient people seem therefore to be intended. It may farther be observed, that the calamities which are referred to are so extensive and general, as to render it in a high degree probable, that the entire body of that people are spoken of. This view is also confirmed, from the introduction of the similitude of a vine transplanted from Egypt. The subject of the psalm may be the same with that of the 79th — the calamitous condition into which the chosen people were brought by the arms of Nebuchadnezzar.
If it is objected, that the ten tribes from the time when they were cut off from the house of David had become degenerate, and that the worship of God was corrupted among them, I answer, that there dwelt among them, notwithstanding, many devout worshippers of God, who had not bowed the knee before Baal, nor abandoned themselves to the prevailing superstition, (1 Kings 19:18.) Accordingly, Amos (Amos 6:6) finds fault with the hard-heartedness which existed in the tribe of Judah, because there was none among them who was “grieved for the affliction of Joseph.” It is also well known, that during the time of this defection, some prophets were sent to them to inspire them with the hope of deliverance. Although, then, the vast proportion of them were apostates, yet God did not cease to exercise his care over the seed which remained in the midst of them. And as formerly he had mitigated coming calamities, by promising beforehand his grace; so now, by dictating to the people a form of prayer, he confirms and encourages them in the hope of obtaining his grace, until they found, from actual experience, that they had not been deceived by vain promises. From this, we perceive in what respect this and the preceding psalm differ from each other. If any one considers what I have now stated unsatisfactory, he is at liberty to adopt a different view. But I flatter myself, that whoever carefully weighs all the circumstances, will readily acquiesce in my opinion. I will not insist upon the words Sosannim and Eduth, having already, in Psalm 45th, stated the opinions of interpreters concerning them; nor is this a matter of so great importance as to render it necessary to expend much labor upon it. Besides, those who are most learned in antiquities adduce nothing but probable conjectures.
Psalm 80:1-3
1. Hearken, O Shepherd of Israel! who leadest Joseph like a flock: thou who sittest between the cherubim, shine forth. 2. In the sight of Ephraim, and Benjamin, and Manasseh, stir up
The original word for “stir up” is, עוררה, orera, from עור, ur, was excited “This word,” says Dimock, “seems to convey the idea of God’s having been asleep during the Babylonish captivity. See Isaiah 51:9.”
thy strength, and come to our deliverance. 3. Turn us again, O God! cause thy face to shine, and we shall be saved.
 
1 Hearken, O Shepherd of Israel! The prophet, previous to his naming Manasseh and Ephraim, makes mention of Joseph; and why does he speak of Joseph rather than of Judah, but because it was his design to treat separately of the kingdom of Israel, the government of which was in the family and posterity of Joseph? Nor, since God sent special prophets among them, after he had stricken them with his rods, is there any inconsistency when, at the same time, the prayer is added, That God would gather together the remnant to himself. Moreover, that they might not delude themselves by trusting in their spurious worship, the prophet, by applying to God the appellation of Him who sitteth between the Cherubim, calls them back to the pure doctrine of the law. The mercy-seat was a pledge of the presence of God, where he had promised to be near his people to hear their prayers. This divinely instituted form, it was unlawful for men to change at their own pleasure. The Israelites, then, are admonished to return to their original state, if they would expect to find God gracious towards them. Besides, by the title which is here attributed to God, there is expressed his wonderful love towards men in humbling, and, so to speak, lowering himself in order to come down to them, and choose for himself a seat and habitation on the earth, that he might dwell in the midst of them. Properly speaking, God cannot be said to sit; nor is it to be supposed that it is possible for him, whom the heaven of heavens cannot contain, to be shut up in a certain place, (1 Kings 8:27.) But, in accommodation to the infirmity of men, he is represented as placed between the two Cherubim, that the faithful might not imagine him to be far from them; and, consequently, be perplexed with doubt and apprehension in approaching him. At the same time, the remark which I have previously made must be borne in mind, that the Israelites are here furnished with a rule for enabling them to pray in a right manner, that they might be withdrawn from the worship of the god fabricated and set up by themselves at Dan and Bethel, and that, rejecting all superstitions, they might yield themselves to be guided by the true light of faith, and follow the Word of God.
